summary: In a fiction excerpt from Book 3, a narrator and a man standing on bluffs overlooking the Hudson River discuss the ancient Greek god Asklepios and his daughter Hygeia, goddess of health. The man contrasts the Asklepian reliance on outside drugs with the Hygeian belief in healing from within, and presents Hygeian herbal and Eastern practices as the basis of his work treating infertility. The narrator, who has had no success with Western medicine, is drawn to his methods but senses he may be too smooth, and the conversation ends with the narrator asking about a woman he met the previous week.
one_line: On the Hudson bluffs, a smooth stranger explains the Hygeian healing tradition and his herbal approach to infertility to a narrator seeking help.
key_facts: The narrator and the man stand on a line of bluffs overlooking the Hudson, where a lone sailboat is caught in the breeze.
The early spring wind is cutting into the narrator's face, causing the nostrils to feel on fire.
The man asks the narrator whether he is familiar with the name Asklepios, and the narrator shakes his head no.
Asklepios is described as the ancient Greek god of medicine.
Physicians who revered Asklepios held that sickness could be cured using drugs and potions that came from outside the body.
Hygeia is described as the daughter of Asklepios and the goddess of health.
The Hygeians believed that wellness originated from properly governing your own body.
The Hygeian ideal was healing from within rather than intervention from without.
The man says the Hygeian school more or less died out in the West but lives on in other places.
The man says primitive peoples have no manufactured, synthetic drugs and use natural herbs to enhance their immune system.
The man states that if a woman is childless, the reason more often than not is that her body is out of harmony with itself.
The man says he seeks out each woman's unique energy flows and attempts to restore them, using Eastern practices and Hygeian herbal therapies.
The narrator says Western medicine had completely struck out for him.
The man says that when a woman's body is naturally unresponsive, he tries to provide her a child by other means, and the narrator suggests adoption.
The narrator says that last week he met a woman who had, and the excerpt ends mid-sentence.
